title: What Does an Insurance Adjuster Do? Staff, Independent, Public
description: What does an insurance adjuster do? Learn the difference between staff, independent, and public adjusters in Texas and who works for you on your claim.
keyword: what does an insurance adjuster do
html:
If you have filed a property claim, you have probably met at least one adjuster, and maybe several. So what does an insurance adjuster do, and who are they actually working for? In Texas there are three main types: staff adjusters, independent adjusters, and public adjusters. The first two work for the insurance company. The third works for you. Understanding the difference helps Galveston homeowners and business owners know what to expect, what to ask, and when to get their own representation.

What Does an Insurance Adjuster Do on a Property Claim?

At its core, an adjuster investigates a claim and determines how much, if anything, the policy should pay. The work typically includes:

  • Reviewing the policy to see what coverages, limits, deductibles, and exclusions apply
  • Inspecting the damage in person or through photos and video
  • Determining the cause of loss, such as wind, hail, fire, water, or flood
  • Writing an estimate, usually with industry estimating software, listing repairs and prices
  • Applying depreciation and the deductible to arrive at a payment amount
  • Requesting documents such as receipts, inventories, and proof of loss
  • Communicating decisions to accept, partially pay, or deny the claim

The short answer to what does an insurance adjuster do is: they measure the loss and apply the policy to it. How that work is done, and on whose behalf, depends on the type of adjuster.

Staff Adjusters

A staff adjuster is an employee of the insurance company. They handle claims for that one carrier and follow its guidelines, pricing, and procedures. Some work from a desk and handle smaller claims by phone and photos. Others are field adjusters who inspect in person.

Who they work for: The insurer.

What to expect: Staff adjusters often have heavy caseloads, especially after a storm. They know the company's policies well but may not have time to catch every detail of your loss.

Independent Adjusters

An independent adjuster is a contractor hired by the insurance company, often through an adjusting firm. After hurricanes and major windstorms on the Texas coast, insurers and TWIA bring in large numbers of independent adjusters, many from out of state, to handle the surge in claims.

Who they work for: The insurer that hired them, despite the word "independent."

What to expect: Independent adjusters inspect the property and write the estimate, but the insurer usually makes the final coverage and payment decision. After a catastrophe, you may see adjuster turnover, where a new adjuster takes over your file partway through.

Public Adjusters

A public adjuster is licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) and is hired by the policyholder. They represent you in the claim process. A public adjuster does many of the same tasks, reviewing the policy, inspecting, documenting, and estimating, but does it to present your claim to the insurer as completely as possible.

Who they work for: You, the policyholder.

What to expect: A public adjuster handles communication with the insurer's adjusters, prepares an independent estimate, organizes documentation, and negotiates the claim. Public adjusters in Texas are typically paid a percentage of the claim payments, under a written contract that must follow state rules. Always verify a public adjuster's license with TDI before signing.

Side-by-Side Comparison

  • Staff adjuster: Employed by the insurer, paid salary by the insurer, represents the insurer.
  • Independent adjuster: Contracted by the insurer, paid by the insurer or adjusting firm, represents the insurer.
  • Public adjuster: Hired by the policyholder, paid by the policyholder under a contract, represents the policyholder.

For a deeper comparison, see our guide on public adjusters versus insurance adjusters, or visit our TWIA claims help page if you have a windstorm claim.

How Adjusters Handle TWIA Claims

The Texas Windstorm Insurance Association, governed by Texas Insurance Code chapter 2210, uses a mix of staff and independent adjusters, especially after a named storm. TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss, and TWIA has its own process for claim decisions and disputes. Because wind and flood are covered by different policies, the adjuster's cause-of-loss determination is especially important on Galveston properties. Our Texas windstorm rules page explains the framework in more detail.

A Typical Claim Timeline

To see what does an insurance adjuster do in practice, it helps to follow a claim from start to finish:

  1. First notice of loss. You report the claim and receive a claim number.
  2. Assignment. The insurer assigns a staff or independent adjuster, who contacts you to schedule an inspection.
  3. Inspection. The adjuster documents the damage with photos, measurements, and notes. Engineers may be called in for roof or structural questions.
  4. Estimate and review. The adjuster writes an estimate, which is often reviewed by a supervisor or desk examiner before a decision is issued.
  5. Decision and payment. You receive a letter explaining what is covered, what is not, and the payment amount after deductible and depreciation.
  6. Supplements. If additional damage is found during repairs, a supplement can be submitted for review.

A public adjuster works alongside this same timeline, but from the policyholder's side, making sure each step has complete information.

What to Ask Any Adjuster Who Inspects Your Property

  1. Who do you work for, and are you staff or independent?
  2. Will you be the adjuster handling my claim through to payment?
  3. Are you inspecting the roof, attic, and every elevation today?
  4. Are you bringing in an engineer or other expert, and will I get a copy of the report?
  5. When will I receive your estimate and photos?
  6. What pricing does your estimate use for this area?
  7. What documents do you need from me, and by when?

Write down the answers and follow up by email so there is a record.

Your Rights During the Adjustment Process

  • You can be present for every inspection.
  • You can take your own photos and notes.
  • You can request a copy of the estimate and the policy.
  • You can submit your own estimate and evidence.
  • Insurers must follow the timelines in the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act, Insurance Code chapter 542.
  • You can hire a licensed public adjuster to represent you.

When Hiring a Public Adjuster Makes Sense

Knowing what does an insurance adjuster do on the insurer's side makes it easier to decide whether you need one on yours. Many small, straightforward claims are resolved fairly without outside help. A public adjuster may be worth considering when:

  • The loss is large, such as a major roof, fire, or hurricane claim
  • The insurer's estimate seems far below repair bids
  • The claim was denied or partially denied
  • Wind and flood coverage are in dispute
  • You do not have the time or expertise to manage the claim

Tools like our shingle wind damage and claim settlement calculators can help you understand your situation before you decide. No adjuster can promise a specific result, but having someone on your side means your side of the claim is documented and presented.

faq.q: What does an insurance adjuster do?
faq.a: An insurance adjuster reviews the policy, inspects the damage, determines the cause of loss, writes a repair estimate, applies depreciation and deductibles, and communicates the claim decision.

faq.q: Is an independent adjuster on my side?
faq.a: No. Independent adjusters are hired by the insurance company and represent the insurer, even though they are not company employees.

faq.q: Who does a public adjuster work for?
faq.a: A public adjuster is hired by and represents the policyholder. In Texas, public adjusters are licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance.
